mappings.note: Pottery as the technology that let settled farmers store surplus - the item asks about the change in SOCIETY, which is a broad development of the ancient period. The bare 'what is this technology called' item is mapped to LO-62 instead.
The Neolithic Revolution enabling settled life is the beginning of agriculture that LO-63 names. Not LO-62, which covers the cultural features of early humans rather than the transition itself.

Stone and shell beads used for adornment, exchange or ritual - a distinctive feature of early human culture. Not LO-59, because the question is about what the ornaments meant, not about their standing as evidence.
Spots the false time term (millennium as ten years) across CE, BCE, century and millennium; a chronology item like the other dating questions.

Reading stratified layers as successive occupations needs both the use of archaeological evidence (LO-59) and the chronological inference drawn from it (LO-65). The plainer 'what is an archaeological source' items take LO-59 alone.
Chipped stone as the material of early cutting tools - a feature of early human culture and technology under LO-62.

Defines culture as the customs, arts and institutions of a people; LO-62 is the only outcome using the word culture, and the chapter introduces the term to describe early human cultures. Not LO-59, no source is involved.
Copper metallurgy giving tools more durable than stone - the growth of early human technology, which LO-62 asks pupils to explain. Not LO-74, whose knowledge of metals is India's own contribution.
Classifies ancient coins as archaeological sources - a source-type identification, so LO-59 rather than the chronology outcome.
Statement set on AD versus CE, the missing year zero and millennium against century: three points of the dating framework, so LO-65.
The Stone Age as the period named after the tool material - a feature of early human culture. Not LO-65, because the item names a cultural stage, not a unit of the calendar.
Agriculture as the turning point that gave stable food supplies; the beginning of agriculture named in LO-63, and the same reading as the Neolithic Revolution item.
Figurines and burial goods are excavated evidence (LO-59) read for what early people believed (LO-62). The item explicitly asks what the archaeologist LEARNS from them, so both halves are needed.
Epigraphy as the study of inscriptions - inscriptions are a source type, and this names the discipline that reads them, so LO-59.
A soldier's diary as a primary literary source: source classification, the 'literary' half of LO-59. Not LO-61, which is about the contents of literary works, not their evidential status.
One-line recall that the study of the human past is History - the goal statement itself, with no source type or development named, so no outcome fits more closely.
Names the geologist among the specialists whose work feeds the reconstruction of the deep past, with the other 'who studies what' items.
Fossils as preserved remains in rock - material evidence of the past, so LO-59. Not LO-62, since the item defines the evidence rather than what it shows about early humans.
The archaeologist digging up tools and pottery - the archaeological source named first in LO-59.
CE as Common Era; part of the dating notation, mapped with the other chronology items.
BCE as Before Common Era - the companion notation to CE, and again a chronology item.
A decade as ten years; the smallest of the chapter's time units, with century and millennium.
A hundred years to the century - a unit of the chronological framework.
A thousand years to the millennium; the same framework at larger scale.
Asks for an Indian literary source such as the Vedas - naming an example of the literary source type in LO-59. Not LO-61, which would apply if the question asked what those texts SAY.
Folklore and genealogy classified as oral sources - a source-type identification under LO-59.
Hunting and gathering as how early humans fed themselves: LO-63 names the hunting-gathering stage outright, which makes it the better fit than LO-62's cultural features.
Caves, rock shelters and temporary camps as early human dwellings - a distinctive feature of early human life, so LO-62 rather than the agricultural transition.
Names pottery as the new clay technology. Mapped to LO-62 because it stops at the invention; the item that asks what pottery CHANGED for society was mapped to LO-63.
Copper as the first metal for durable tools - the same technological growth as the metallurgy item, under LO-62.
A hamlet as the smallest settlement; settlement vocabulary belonging to the shift to settled life that LO-63 covers.

Defines 'afterlife', the belief the chapter infers from burial goods - part of the distinctive features of early human culture in LO-62. Not LO-75, whose religions and systems of thought are those of the later ancient period.

Why knowing the past explains the present - the rationale for the whole subject, stated at goal level. No outcome covers the value of history as such; LO-59 concerns sources and LO-65 concerns chronology.
Distinguishes the geologist's rocks from the palaeontologist's fossils; a discrimination among the specialists who supply evidence, so LO-59.
Why the religiously neutral CE replaced AD - a point about the dating convention itself, hence LO-65.
Computes 199 years between 100 BCE and 100 CE, allowing for the missing year zero; the sharpest chronology calculation in the chapter.
How a time line clarifies sequence, duration and relation between events - the purpose of chronological synthesis in LO-65.
Defines oral sources and asks for two examples; a source-type item, longer than the multiple-choice version but the same outcome.
DNA, chemical and palaeoclimate analysis adding to the evidence base - new source types and their use in reconstructing the past, which is LO-59's second clause.
